analysis.investment_thesis: Shanmuga Hospital fails the Magic Formula decisively: a 0.15% ROE signals almost no return on capital, and while the 12.2 P/E implies a ~8% earnings yield, neither leg of the "cheap and good" framework is satisfied. A tiny single-hospital operator in Salem with negligible profitability is the opposite of the quality-at-a-discount setup I hunt for.
key_strengths: P/E of 12.2 is not egregiously expensive in absolute terms
Hospital industry has structural tailwinds in tier-2 India
key_risks: ROE of 0.15% indicates near-zero return on capital — fails Magic Formula quality test
Tiny INR 46.8 Cr market cap single-hospital business lacks scale and moat
Incorporated only in 2020 — no 3+ year track record of sustained ROIC
red_flags: ROE effectively zero (0.15%) — the entire point of the Magic Formula is high ROIC
Hospital businesses are capital-intensive; low ROE here suggests capex is destroying returns
No FII participation and microcap size → liquidity and governance risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula lens, the single most important number here is ROE of 0.15%. Hospitals are working-capital light but fixed-asset heavy, and a return that low means EBIT/(NWC+Net Fixed Assets) is almost certainly in the low single digits — nowhere near the >20% threshold I require for the "good business" half of the formula. The P/E of 12.2 translates to an earnings yield of roughly 8%, which is decent but not exceptional, and without the ROIC to back it up, cheapness alone doesn't qualify. Cheap-and-mediocre is a value trap, not a bargain.

The company is a freshly incorporated (2020) single-location Salem hospital with a INR 46.8 Cr market cap — too small, too young, and too unproven to pass a systematic screen. Promoter holding of 72% is the one positive, but it doesn't compensate for a business earning essentially nothing on its capital base. I'd pass and redeploy capital into names that rank in the top decile on both earnings yield AND return on capital.
